# The Kestrel Islands — field notes, part 1: geography

*Invented material. See the README of the demo project.*

The Kestrel Islands are an archipelago of five inhabited islands and a
scattering of rocks that nobody bothers to count. They lie in the Ashwind Sea,
roughly 400 km from the nearest mainland harbour.

## The five islands

| Island   | Area (km²) | Inhabitants | Main settlement |
|----------|-----------:|------------:|-----------------|
| Torvig   |        410 |       3 200 | Torvig Harbour  |
| Little Kestrel | 96   |         840 | Fenmouth        |
| Skarn    |        155 |         210 | Skarn Landing   |
| Ovray    |         62 |         115 | Ovray Cove      |
| Bellhorn |         18 |           0 | (lighthouse only) |

Torvig is the largest and the only island with a deep-water pier. Everything
that arrives in the archipelago arrives there first and is redistributed by the
mail boat.

## Relief

The islands are the rim of a drowned volcanic crater. The rim is highest in the
north-west, where Skarn rises to 612 m at the Skarn Ridge, and lowest in the
south, where Ovray barely reaches 40 m. The crater floor between the islands is
the Kestrel Deep, 890 m at its deepest sounding.

Bellhorn is not part of the rim: it is a basalt plug, vertical on three sides,
and carries the only lighthouse of the archipelago. It has been uninhabited
since the light was automated.

## Settlements

Torvig Harbour holds two thirds of the population of the archipelago. Fenmouth
on Little Kestrel is the second settlement and the seat of the tide office.
Skarn Landing and Ovray Cove are villages of a few dozen houses each; both are
reachable only by boat, and Ovray Cove only at high water.

## Weather

The prevailing wind is the ashwind, a dry north-easterly that blows for about
200 days a year and gives the sea its name. Fog is common in the two weeks
around the spring equinox, when warm air from the south meets the cold water
over the Kestrel Deep.
